sentence: The treasure chest held only ___ pennies, hardly worth the long voyage.
explanation: From an old Low German word, palte, meaning 'rags, trash.' A paltry tip is practically trash.

sentence: Safety is ___ — the most important thing of all — when handling fireworks.
explanation: From French par amont, 'up the mountain' (monte). Paramount means at the very top, which is why the Paramount Pictures logo is a mountain peak!

sentence: Instead of fighting back, the ___ prisoner just accepted whatever happened.
explanation: Italian passivo, from patire, 'to endure.' A passive person lets things happen to them instead of acting.

sentence: The ___ teacher noticed right away that Peter was upset, even though he was smiling.
explanation: Italian percepire, 'to perceive.' Perceptive people take in everything and notice what others miss.

sentence: The neighbors' ___ feud over a single fallen leaf lasted three years.
explanation: From French petit, 'small,' as in petite. Petty arguments are about small, silly things.

sentence: The ___ of the stranded whales touched hearts around the world.
explanation: From an old French word for 'condition.' It rhymes with fright: a plight is a frightening fix, like a kitten stuck in a tree.

sentence: Instead of dreaming of a mansion, the ___ couple bought a small house they could afford.
explanation: From Greek pragma, 'a deed, a thing done,' like practical and practice. Pragmatic people care about what actually works.

sentence: Winning the Nobel Prize brought the scientist great ___.
explanation: Italian prestigio, and a prestigiatore is a magician! The word first meant dazzling trickery; now it means dazzling respect.

sentence: In the end, good will ___ over evil.
explanation: Italian prevalere: to be stronger (valere), to win. Prevalent comes from the same root.

sentence: At age five, the piano ___ was already playing concerts around the world.
explanation: Italian prodigio, 'a marvel.' A prodigy is a young marvel, like Mozart writing music at age five.

sentence: The ___ author wrote over two hundred books.
explanation: From prole, 'offspring,' + fare. A prolific author makes book after book, like having lots of kids.

sentence: The ___ village had cobblestone streets, thatched roofs, and a tiny tea shop.
explanation: From an old French word for 'clever, pretty,' from the root of conoscere, 'to know.' Today quaint means charmingly old-fashioned.

sentence: Only a tall glass of lemonade could ___ Quinn's thirst on the scorching day.
explanation: From Old English acwencan, 'to put out a fire.' Quench rhymes with drench: drench a fire to put it out, drench your thirst with water.

sentence: The knights set out on a long ___ to find the hidden golden goblet.
explanation: Same root as chiedere, inchiesta, and conquista: to seek. A quest is a long search, like a knight's quest for treasure.

sentence: After years of practice, Priya became ___ at the violin.
explanation: From the root of profitto: in Italian school, con profitto means 'with real progress.' A proficient swimmer has made real progress.

sentence: The freshly fallen snow was ___, without a single footprint.
explanation: From the root of ripristinare, 'to restore to the original.' Pristine things are still in their original condition.

sentence: The police arrived to ___ the riot and restore order.
explanation: From Old English cwellan, 'to kill,' a cousin of German quälen, 'to torment.' To quell a riot or a fear is to stamp it out.

sentence: Rumors ran ___ through the school, spreading faster than anyone could stop them.
explanation: Italian rampante, 'rearing up,' like arrampicarsi, 'to climb.' On a coat of arms, a lion rampant rears up. Rampant things run wild.

sentence: The ___ crows cawed loudly and harshly outside my window at dawn.
explanation: Italian rauco, 'hoarse.' A raucous crowd yells until everyone is hoarse.

sentence: After the flood, the waters began to slowly ___.
explanation: Italian recedere: to go back, give way (cedere). The tide recedes, and so does a receding hairline.

sentence: The store promised to ___ the mistake and refund our money.
explanation: Italian rettificare, from retto, 'straight, right' (as in rettangolo). To rectify is to make right.

sentence: The scientist used solid data to ___ the claim that the Earth is flat.
explanation: Italian confutare, 'to disprove.' To refute a claim, you knock it down with proof.

sentence: Let me ___: do NOT open the door. I repeat: do NOT open the door.
explanation: Italian reiterare. Reiterate already means 'say again,' so saying 'reiterate again' is repeating yourself!

sentence: The chef won ___ across the country for her famous pies.
explanation: Italian rinomato, 'renowned,' from nome: your name repeated everywhere.

sentence: After the party, we had to ___ the fridge with fresh food.
explanation: re- 'again' + pieno, 'full': to fill up again, like riempire. You replenish the snack drawer.

sentence: Rita was ___ about her past, rarely revealing anything about herself.
explanation: Italian reticente, from tacere, 'to be silent' (Taci!). A reticent person keeps their thoughts to themselves.

sentence: The newspaper had to ___ the false story and print an apology.
explanation: Italian ritrarre, from trarre, 'to pull' (as in trattore). Cats retract their claws, and you can retract what you said.

sentence: The judge can ___ your license if you drive recklessly.
explanation: Italian revocare: to call back (voce). To revoke a license is to call it back.

sentence: The cave dwellers' ___ tools were just simple sticks and stones.
explanation: From rudimenti, 'the basics,' related to rude, 'rough.' Rudimentary skills are just the rough basics.

sentence: The king refused to ___ his crown, even when the people demanded it.
explanation: From the same root as delinquente (someone who abandons their duty): to leave behind. To relinquish is to let go.

sentence: The younger kids ___ always getting the hand-me-down clothes.
explanation: Italian risentire, risentimento: to feel (sentire) the hurt again and again.

sentence: When Rob asked her to dance, Rita chose to ___ him with a curt “No thanks.”
explanation: From Italian ribuffo, 'a scolding,' related to buffo, 'a puff.' A rebuff is a quick puff that blows someone away.

sentence: A nap and a smoothie can ___ even the most tired traveler.
explanation: Like ringiovanire, from giovane, 'young': to make young again. A nap can rejuvenate you.

sentence: The village ___ sat under the old tree, offering wise advice to all who asked.
explanation: Italian saggio, 'wise,' from sapere, 'to know.' A sage is a wise old person, like Yoda.

sentence: The divers tried to ___ the treasure from the sunken ship before the storm hit.
explanation: From salvare, 'to save.' Divers salvage treasure from a sunken ship.

sentence: The proud queen treated the peasants with ___, as if they were dirt beneath her shoes.
explanation: Same family as Italian scherno, schernire, 'to mock.' Picture someone wrinkling their nose in scorn at soggy fries.

sentence: After losing the game, Sol found ___ in a big bowl of ice cream.
explanation: From the root of consolare, 'to comfort.' A hug is solace after a bad day.

sentence: The snooty princess chose to ___ every suitor's proposal with a sneer.
explanation: From Old English spurnan, 'to kick away,' related to spur, the spike on a rider's heel (German Sporn). To spurn someone is to kick them away.

definition: ability to keep going for a long time
sentence: Running a marathon takes incredible ___ to keep going mile after mile.
explanation: From stame, 'thread.' The ancients pictured the Fates spinning the thread of your life; a strong thread means you can last a long time.

sentence: The ___ dog stayed loyally by his owner's side through every storm.
explanation: stead 'place' (German Statt, Stätte) + fast 'firm' (German fest). Steadfast means fixed in place and not budging.

sentence: Years of ___ between the two kingdoms left both of them in ruins.
explanation: From old French estrif, which came from a Germanic word, a cousin of German Streit, 'quarrel.' Strife is everyone striving against each other.

sentence: With no fresh water flowing in, the ___ pond turned green and smelly.
explanation: From stagno, 'a pond.' Stagnant water just sits there and doesn't flow, and neither does a stagnant career.

sentence: Stan, the team's most ___ supporter, cheers even when they lose every game.
explanation: From old French estanche, 'watertight,' like Italian stagno in a tenuta stagna. A staunch ship doesn't leak, and a staunch friend doesn't waver.

definition: quiet and secret to avoid notice
sentence: The ___ cat crept silently toward the unsuspecting mouse.
explanation: steal + -th + -y; steal is a cousin of German stehlen. Stealth jets sneak past radar like a thief.

sentence: Sitting in the silent library, Stella tried to ___ a giggle.
explanation: From Old French estouffer, 'to smother.' You stifle a yawn by smothering it.

definition: enduring pain without complaint or emotion
sentence: The ___ soldier didn't flinch or complain, even with a broken arm.
explanation: From Greek stoa, 'porch.' The Stoic philosophers taught on a painted porch in Athens, and they taught people to stay calm through pain and trouble.

sentence: Her ___ summary was just one sentence, but it said everything.
explanation: Italian succinto, from cinta and cintura, 'belt.' Romans belted up their robes so nothing flapped around, and succinct writing is belted up tight.

sentence: The ___ teenager slumped silently in the back seat, scowling at everyone.
explanation: From the root of solo, 'alone.' A sullen kid sulks alone in silence.

sentence: The tenth spoon at the place setting was ___; nobody needs that many spoons.
explanation: Italian superfluo: overflowing (super + fluire). Superfluous things are extra, more than needed.

sentence: The ___ farmer rarely said more than “Yep” or “Nope.”
explanation: Italian taciturno, from tacere: Taci! A taciturn person barely says a word.

sentence: Instead of saying “You look terrible,” the ___ friend asked, “Are you feeling okay?”
explanation: Italian tatto, 'touch, tact'; German Takt, as in Taktgefühl, a feel for what to say. A tactful person handles feelings with a gentle touch.

sentence: The island's ___ climate never gets too hot or too cold.
explanation: Italian temperato, 'mild, moderate,' like temperatura. A temperate climate is never too hot or too cold.

sentence: The boss's ___ reply was a single word: “No.”
explanation: From tergere, 'to wipe,' as in tergicristallo (windshield wiper) and detergente! A terse reply has been wiped clean of every extra word.

sentence: The ___ glass let us see every fish in the aquarium.
explanation: Italian trasparente: light appears (apparire) through it, like glass.

definition: fear or worry about what may happen
sentence: With great ___, Trent tiptoed into the haunted house.
explanation: Italian trepidazione, from trepidare, 'to tremble.' Intrepid means without trembling. Trepidation makes your knees shake.

sentence: Smartphones are ___ these days; you see them literally everywhere.
explanation: Italian ubiquo, from Latin ubique, 'everywhere.' Smartphones are ubiquitous: they're everywhere you look.

sentence: The robot's ___ resemblance to Grandma gave everyone the creeps.
explanation: un- 'not' + canny, 'knowing,' a cousin of German kennen and können. Something uncanny is beyond knowing: weird and eerie.

definition: large and awkward to carry or use
sentence: The ___ couch was so bulky we couldn't fit it through the door.
explanation: cumber, 'to weigh down' (as in encumber), + -some. German Kummer, 'worry,' is a cousin that once meant a heap of rubble. A cumbersome suitcase weighs you down.

sentence: The two rivals exchanged ___ greetings, polite and warm.
explanation: Italian cordiale, from cuore, 'heart.' A cordial greeting comes from the heart.

definition: careful and hardworking; wishing to do right
sentence: The ___ student always double-checked her homework and never forgot to hand it in.
explanation: From coscienza, built on the root of scienza, 'knowing.' A conscientious student listens to their conscience and does the work right.

sentence: The angry coach would ___ the referee loudly for every bad call.
explanation: be- 'thoroughly' + rate, an old verb meaning 'to scold.' To berate is to scold someone thoroughly.

sentence: Spreading rumors behind her back will ___ the captain's authority.
explanation: under + mine; German unterminieren means the same. Attackers dug mines (tunnels) under castle walls to collapse them, so to undermine is to weaken from below.

sentence: The town saw ___ snowfall in July, something that had never happened before.
explanation: Like senza precedenti: nothing like it has ever come before.

sentence: The ___ chemical could explode at the slightest shake.
explanation: From volare, 'to fly' (and in Italian, i volatili are birds!). Volatile chemicals fly off into the air; volatile tempers fly off the handle.

sentence: The soap bubble's beauty was ___, popping a second after it formed.
explanation: Greek epi- 'on' + hemera 'day'; effimero in Italian. Mayflies, which live about a day, are called Ephemeroptera.

sentence: Fearing punishment, Fabian decided to ___ a story about aliens stealing his homework.
explanation: From fabbrica (German Fabrik), 'factory.' To fabricate is to build something, including a made-up story.

sentence: The choir sang in perfect ___, every voice blending beautifully.
explanation: From Greek harmonia, 'a joining, agreement.' In music, harmony is notes that fit together, like on a harmonica.

sentence: The note was ___: “The owl hoots twice at the broken clock.”
explanation: From Greek kryptos, 'hidden.' A crypt is a hidden underground room, and cryptography is secret code. Cryptic messages hide their meaning.

sentence: The spies carried out their ___ mission, hidden from the enemy.
explanation: From the same root as coperto, 'covered.' Covert operations are under cover. The opposite is overt.

sentence: The clerk's ___ reply, “Next!”, made it clear he didn't want to chat.
explanation: From corto, 'short.' A curt reply is rudely cut short: 'Fine.'

sentence: The senate voted to formally ___ the senator for breaking the rules.
explanation: Italian censura, from the Roman censor, an official who judged people's behavior (and counted them in the census).

sentence: The school will not ___ cheating of any kind.
explanation: Italian condonare, 'to forgive a debt or fine' (un condono). To condone is to give bad behavior a pass.

sentence: Three witnesses came forward to ___ Cora's story.
explanation: Italian corroborare, from the root of rovere, 'oak' (as in robusto). To corroborate a story is to make it stronger with evidence.

sentence: The camera footage showed who was ___: the dog, with frosting on his nose.
explanation: From colpa, 'fault, blame.' A culprit is the one to blame, and 'mea culpa' means 'my fault.'

sentence: The ___ puppy hung its head after chewing up the shoe, looking truly sorry.
explanation: Italian contrito, from the root of trito, 'ground down.' A contrite person feels crushed by guilt.

sentence: I ___ with your opinion completely; you're absolutely right.
explanation: Italian concorrere: to run (correre) together. When you concur, your opinions run together.

sentence: Be ___ of the slippery floor, and walk carefully.
explanation: From the root of conoscere, 'to know' (as in incognito). To be cognizant is to know about something.

sentence: The comedian's joke was meant to ___ laughter from the crowd.
explanation: From the same root as allettare, 'to lure.' A joke elicits a laugh by luring it out. Don't confuse it with illicit (illegal).

sentence: The ___ split gave each of the four kids exactly the same number of cookies.
explanation: From equo, 'fair,' related to uguale. An equitable split gives everyone a fair share.

sentence: Paying extra will ___ shipping, so your package arrives tomorrow.
explanation: ex- 'out' + piede, 'foot': freeing the feet so things move fast. Italian spedire, 'to ship,' comes straight from it. It's the opposite of impede.

sentence: Food critics love to ___ the chef's famous pie, praising it to the skies.
explanation: ex- 'up' + tollere 'to lift.' To extol is to lift someone up high with praise.

definition: a mistaken belief or faulty reasoning
sentence: It's a common ___ that goldfish have three-second memories; it isn't true.
explanation: From the root of fallire and falso: to fail, to fool. A fallacy is an idea that fools you.

sentence: The knight's ___ to his king never wavered.
explanation: Italian fedeltà, from fede, 'faith' (Fido, the faithful dog's name). Old stereos said 'hi-fi': high fidelity, sound faithful to the original.

definition: free from a duty or rule; release from
sentence: Seniors are ___ from the final exam, free to skip it.
explanation: Italian esente, 'exempt.' If you're exempt from the test, you've been taken out of it.

sentence: The storyteller's tale will ___ the campers, holding them spellbound around the fire.
explanation: en- + thrall, an old word for a servant or captive. An enthralling book holds you captive.

sentence: Don't ___ yourself into thinking you can study for the test in five minutes.
explanation: Same root as Italian deludere. Careful: deludere means to disappoint; English delude means to fool someone into a false belief.

sentence: A good coach will never ___ players by calling them names.
explanation: de- 'down' + mean 'low, poor.' To demean someone is to drag their dignity down low.

definition: speak of as unimportant or bad
sentence: Sore losers often ___ the winners, calling their victory “pure luck.”
explanation: Built on pari, 'equal': putting someone below their equals. To disparage something is to put it down below its worth.

definition: insisting one's beliefs are certainly right
sentence: The ___ professor insisted his theory was absolutely right and refused to consider any other.
explanation: From Greek dogma, 'a belief' (nothing to do with dogs). But picture a dog with a bone: a dogmatic person won't let go of their belief.

sentence: The desert town's ___ of water was so severe that every well had run dry.
explanation: dear + -th, like warm + -th = warmth. Dear once meant 'costly,' like German teuer: when something is scarce, it becomes dear.

sentence: Let's ___ the decision until tomorrow, when everyone is less tired.
explanation: Italian differire, 'to put off.' To defer is to put something off until later, or to put your opinion aside out of respect (deference).

definition: separate and go in different directions
sentence: At the fork, the two paths ___, one heading north and the other south.
explanation: Italian divergere: di- 'apart' + a root meaning 'to bend, turn.' Roads that diverge bend away from each other. Converge (convergere) means coming together.

definition: make room for; adapt to fit someone's needs
sentence: The hotel can ___ up to five hundred guests.
explanation: From comodo, 'comfortable, convenient.' To accommodate is to make room for. Spelling trick: it makes room for two c's and two m's.

sentence: Teasing the cat will only ___ her, and then she'll scratch you.
explanation: Greek anti- 'against' + agon 'struggle' (as in agony). The antagonist of a story struggles against the hero.

sentence: The movie's ___ plot was one we'd all seen a hundred times before.
explanation: Italian banale, the same word. It first meant shared by the whole village (one mill, one oven): so common that it's boring.

sentence: The busy nurse gave one ___ nod and hurried off without a word.
explanation: From Italian brusco, 'sour, sharp.' A brusque person brushes you off sharply.

sentence: The ___ beach ball bobbed happily on the waves.
explanation: buoy (a floating marker) + -ant. Buoys float, and a buoyant mood floats too.

sentence: The ___ essay used five hundred words to say what could be said in five.
explanation: From verbo, 'word,' + -ose 'full of.' Verbose writing is stuffed full of words.

sentence: The ___ crowd pushed and shoved past the barriers.
explanation: un- 'not' + rule + -y. Unruly kids don't follow the rules. Picture unruly hair sticking up everywhere.

sentence: Judges must ___ the law, even when it's unpopular.
explanation: up + hold: to hold something up. Judges uphold the law.

sentence: The hero swore to ___ the dragon once and for all.
explanation: From vincere, 'to win, conquer.' Julius Caesar said, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.

sentence: Many people ___ the ancient temple as a holy place.
explanation: Italian venerare, 'to worship, honor.' Venerable means worthy of deep respect, like a wise old tree.

sentence: The fly buzzing around my head continued to ___ me all afternoon.
explanation: Italian vessare, 'to harass.' Vex rhymes with hex: a vexing problem feels like it's cursed.

sentence: The DNA test will ___ the accused man, proving his innocence.
explanation: Same root as vendicare, 'to avenge.' When you're vindicated, you're freed from blame because you've been proven right.

sentence: The ___ fox tricked the crow into dropping its cheese.
explanation: wile 'a trick' + -y. Think of Wile E. Coyote, always plotting wily tricks to catch the Road Runner.

sentence: Since the move, Will had become quiet and ___, spending all his time alone in his room.
explanation: with 'back, away' (as in withhold) + drawn. A withdrawn person has drawn back into themselves, like a turtle in its shell.

sentence: The children fled from the ___ of the giant whose garden they'd trampled.
explanation: From Old English wraeth, 'anger.' Wrath is fury so big it's one of the old 'seven deadly sins.'

sentence: Stuck in the city, the old sailors ___ for the open sea.
explanation: A cousin of German gern and begehren, 'to desire.' You yearn all year for summer vacation.

sentence: Zoe attacked her science project with ___, working day and night with great enthusiasm.
explanation: From Greek zelos, 'eagerness': zelo in Italian. The same word gave us geloso, 'jealous.' Zealous people are full of zeal.

sentence: The ___ lumberjack carried two logs on each shoulder.
explanation: From Middle English borli, 'stately, sturdy.' Picture a burly lumberjack with huge shoulders.

definition: mix up so as to make unclear
sentence: A bad phone connection can ___ your message into nonsense.
explanation: From Italian garbellare, 'to sift,' borrowed from Arabic gharbala. Sift a message badly and you mix it all up.

sentence: The ___ neon-pink-and-lime-green suit hurt everyone's eyes.
explanation: Possibly from an old word, gaure, 'to stare.' Garish colors are so loud and flashy that people stare.

definition: talking too much about trivial things
sentence: The ___ barber chatted endlessly about the weather, his cat, and his cousin's new car.
explanation: Italian garrulo, 'chattering.' Picture a garrulous parrot that never stops chattering about nothing.

sentence: Good grades will ___ your parents, pleasing them greatly.
explanation: From grato, 'thankful,' the root of grazie! Gratifying work pleases you.

sentence: After three sleepless nights, the new parents looked pale and ___.
explanation: It first meant a wild hawk caught as an adult, which looked scrawny and wild. A haggard person looks worn out and ragged.

sentence: The ___ cat spent all day lying in the sun, too lazy to chase mice.
explanation: in- 'not' + dolore, 'pain': not wanting to feel any effort. Indolent means lazy.

sentence: The ___ buzz of the mosquito kept me up all night.
explanation: irk + -some, from Middle English irken, 'to be weary of.' An irksome itch irks you all day.

sentence: The rude fans began to ___ at the losing team as they left the field.
explanation: It rhymes with cheer and sneer: a jeer is a sneering, rude cheer, like booing.

definition: a person who wanders with no fixed home
sentence: The desert ___ moved his tent from oasis to oasis, never settling down.
explanation: From Greek nomas, 'wandering to find pasture.' Nomads move from place to place with their herds.

sentence: The ___ picture frame was covered in carved gold flowers, swirls, and cherubs.
explanation: Italian ornato, 'decorated,' like ornamento. Ornate furniture is covered in decorations.

sentence: The players voted to ___ the captain and pick a new one.
explanation: From old French ouster, 'to remove,' from the same root as ostacolo, 'obstacle.' Hear it as 'out': to oust someone is to kick them out.

sentence: With enough ketchup, even the cafeteria meatloaf was ___.
explanation: From palato, 'palate' (where you taste), + -able. Palatable food is pleasant to taste, and palatable ideas are easy to swallow.

definition: strongly supporting one side; a supporter
sentence: The ___ crowd booed every call that went against the home team.
explanation: Italian partigiano, from parte: someone who takes one side. In World War II, i partigiani fought for their side in the Resistance.

sentence: The ___ thief returned the stolen goods and begged for forgiveness.
explanation: Same root as pentirsi, 'to repent.' A penitent person is sorry for what they did.

definition: steal goods by force; stolen goods
sentence: The pirates came ashore to ___ the village, taking every coin and candlestick.
explanation: From German plündern, 'to loot,' from Plunder, 'household stuff, junk.' Pirates plunder: they take all the stuff.

definition: having a strong, sharp smell or taste
sentence: The ___ smell of the blue cheese filled the whole house.
explanation: From pungere, 'to sting, prick.' A pungent smell stings your nose.

sentence: The ___ passenger whined and complained about everything during the entire flight.
explanation: From the root of querela, a formal complaint. German has a great word for a querulous person: ein Querulant, someone who complains about everything.

sentence: The butter had gone ___, smelling sour and spoiled.
explanation: Italian rancido, 'gone bad.' Rancid butter smells rank.

sentence: The states voted to ___ the new amendment, making it official.
explanation: Italian ratificare, 'to confirm officially.' To ratify a treaty is to make it officially settled.

sentence: Saying “free gift” is ___; all gifts are free.
explanation: Italian ridondante, from onda, 'wave,' the same root as abundant. Redundant words spill over: 'free gift,' 'tuna fish.'

sentence: The prince chose to ___ his claim to the throne and become a farmer.
explanation: Italian rinunciare, 'to give up.' To renounce something is to announce you're giving it up.

sentence: The league must officially ___ the new rule before teams can use it.
explanation: From santo, 'holy, made binding' (sanzione). A sanction can be official approval, or a penalty for breaking the rules: a word with two opposite meanings!

definition: too eager to obey or please
sentence: The ___ butler bowed and scraped, eager to fulfill his master's every whim.
explanation: From servo, 'servant,' and servire. A servile person acts like a servant, too eager to obey.

sentence: The ___ rain fell in short bursts, on and off all day.
explanation: From Greek sporadikos, 'scattered' (spora, 'seed'); sporadico in Italian. Sporadic rain falls in scattered bits, like seeds tossed here and there.

sentence: The gymnast's ___ body could bend into a pretzel.
explanation: From the root of piegare, 'to bend, fold' (and supplicare, to kneel and beg). A supple gymnast bends and folds easily.

sentence: The con man tried to ___ the old lady out of her savings.
explanation: From German Schwindler, 'a cheat,' from Schwindel, 'dizziness.' A swindler makes your head spin while taking your money.

sentence: The ___ accountant checked every number twice and would never cheat.
explanation: From scrupolo (German Skrupel), which first meant a tiny sharp pebble: like a pebble in your shoe, a little worry about doing right. Scrupulous people pay attention to it.

sentence: The ___ puppy rolled over and showed its belly to the bigger dog.
explanation: sub- 'under' + mettere, 'to put,' like sottomesso. A submissive person puts themselves under someone else's control.

sentence: Without any evidence to ___ his claim, no one believed Sam had seen Bigfoot.
explanation: From sostanza, 'substance' (sub + stare, 'to stand under'). To substantiate a claim is to give it solid ground to stand on.

definition: sharply insightful; sees what others miss
sentence: Percy the ___ owl peered past the fox's fake smile and spotted the plot before anyone else.
explanation: Italian perspicace, the same word, from a root meaning 'to see through.' A perspicacious person sees right through things.

definition: hard to control, manage, or solve
sentence: The ___ knot in the kite string defeated fingers, forks, and Dad's best efforts — nobody could undo it.
explanation: Italian intrattabile: not trattabile, 'able to be handled' (trattare). An intractable problem can't be handled.

sentence: The ___ peacock puffed out his chest and paraded around as if he owned the whole park.
explanation: From pompa, a showy parade (in pompa magna); German says pompös. A pompous person struts like they're leading a parade.
